Short answer
- Consider an LED task lamp with integrated LED (not an old halogen/incandescent), dimming, 4000–5000 K color temperature, CRI ≥ 80, and an efficacy ≥ 70–90 lm/W. From your catalog memory I found a product named "Meadowlight Lamp" that would be a natural first candidate to check — but I don’t have its technical specs in memory, so you’ll need to verify the details below.

What to look for (why each matters)
- Integrated LED (or an LED module): LEDs use far less electricity than incandescent/halogen for the same light output. Evidence: many lab and industry studies show LEDs need ~10–20% of the energy of an incandescent for comparable lumens. Claim to verify: the Meadowlight (or any specific lamp) actual wattage and lumen output.
- Lumens and efficacy (lm/W): Look for the lamp’s total lumens and divide by watts to get lm/W. Target at least ~70 lm/W (higher is better). Evidence: efficacy directly measures energy efficiency. Claim to verify: the lamp’s stated lumens and watts on the spec sheet or label.
- Color temperature: 4000–5000 K is good for focused office tasks (neutral to cool white). Evidence: common lighting practice and standards for task lighting. Claim to verify: the lamp’s listed CCT (correlated color temperature).
- CRI (Color Rendering Index) ≥ 80: Important so colors on documents/screens appear natural. Evidence: industry guidance recommends CRI≥80 for offices. Claim to verify: lamp’s CRI reported in specs.
- Dimmable driver and dimming type (triac, 0–10V, PWM, etc.): Dimming saves energy and reduces glare; check the compatibility with your dimmer system if you already have one. Claim to verify: that the Meadowlight model is truly dimmable and which dimming protocol it uses.
- Controls and sensors: Motion/occupancy sensors, timers, and task-level controls (head swivel, brightness memory) can add savings and convenience. Evidence: control strategies reduce run-hours, saving energy. Claim to verify: actual controls included with the model.
- Certifications: ENERGY STAR or DesignLights Consortium (DLC) listings indicate verified efficiency in many regions. Claim to verify: whether the specific lamp model is ENERGY STAR/DLC listed.
- Warranty and expected life (L70 hours): Longer warranted lifetimes reduce replacement frequency and lifecycle energy/materials cost. Claim to verify: stated life (e.g., 50,000 hours) and warranty terms.

How to map lamp specs to an office desk
- Typical task lighting target: ~300–500 lux on the work surface. For a single desk lamp you’ll usually want ~400–800 lumens directed to the task area (exact needs depend on desk area, reflectances, and whether you have overhead light). Evidence: lighting design guidelines. Claim to verify: specific lux requirements for your tasks and the lamp’s beam and distribution.

Quick example of energy savings (illustrative)
- Replacing a 60 W incandescent desk lamp with a 10 W LED that delivers similar task light saves ~50 W. Over 1,800 office hours/year that’s ~90 kWh/year saved per lamp. (Cost savings depend on local electricity rates.) Claim to verify: actual wattage/lumen equivalence of the Meadowlight (or chosen lamp) and your actual hours of use.

1. If you want a single model to evaluate first: check the Meadowlight Lamp spec sheet for:
   - LED (integrated) or LED-specified bulb
   - Watts and total lumens (calculate lm/W)
   - CCT (aim 4000–5000 K) and CRI ≥ 80
   - Dimmable? Which dimming protocol?
   - ENERGY STAR or DLC listing
   - Warranty and rated life (e.g., 50,000 hours)
2. If Meadowlight doesn’t meet those, look for other adjustable LED task lamps with the same spec targets.
3. If you want, I can:
   - Look up Meadowlight Lamp specs if you give me a link or SKU, or if you want me to search the web (I’ll need permission to use live web search).
